title: 2025 International Engagement Fair
location: Courtyard, Gunn SIEPR Building, 366 Galvez Street
host: King Center on Global Development, Bing Overseas Studies Program, Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies, Global Engineering Programs, and Stanford Global Studies
audience: Stanford students
summary: A campus fair connecting Stanford students with international study, research, professional experiences, and student organizations.
description: Stanford students explored organizations offering academic and professional experiences abroad, international activities on campus, and other forms of international exchange. The fair brought campus programs and student groups together in the Gunn SIEPR courtyard.

The King Center on Global Development co-hosted the fair with Bing Overseas Studies, FSI, Global Engineering Programs, and Stanford Global Studies. KIDA participated in the event as part of its student engagement activities.

title: Research Roadmap: Fieldwork in Fragile States
location: Doll 320, third floor, Gunn SIEPR Building
host: King Center on Global Development
audience: Graduate students interested in global development
summary: Michael Callen shared practical guidance for field research in fragile states and unpredictable political settings.
description: Michael Callen drew on his experience conducting fieldwork during political uncertainty and working with vulnerable populations. He discussed how students can approach research in complex settings and adapt to unpredictable conditions.

The conversation also introduced his work using a new framework and AI to assess institutional uncertainty across countries and history. It formed part of the King Center's Research Roadmap series for graduate students pursuing global development research.

title: Global Health Opportunities Fair
location: LKSC 101/102, Li Ka Shing Center, Stanford Medical School
host: Stanford Undergraduate Global Health Club and Stanford Graduate Global Health Network, with the Center for Innovation in Global Health and Bay Area Global Health Alliance
audience: Students interested in global health research, internships, volunteering, and projects
summary: Students met global health researchers and organizations offering internships, research projects, and ways to contribute.
description: The fair connected students interested in global health with faculty, researchers, NGOs, and industry organizations. Participants could explore internships, research and publication projects, volunteer roles, and other ways to gain experience while supporting global health work.

The Stanford Undergraduate Global Health Club and Graduate Global Health Network hosted the fair with support from the Center for Innovation in Global Health and Bay Area Global Health Alliance. KIDA's involvement is recorded in the organization's event history supplied for this website.

title: Lunch with Professor Claire Adida
location: Doll 320, Gunn SIEPR Building
host: King International Development Association (KIDA)
audience: Students
summary: KIDA invited students to lunch with FSI Senior Fellow and CDDRL affiliate Professor Claire Adida.
description: KIDA hosted a lunch conversation with Professor Claire Adida, introduced on the original invitation as an FSI Senior Fellow and CDDRL affiliate. The gathering took place in Doll 320 in the Gunn SIEPR Building on Monday, November 10, 2025.
Lunch was provided. The invitation does not publish a start time or a specific discussion theme.

title: Innovation Through Social Enterprise
location: Koret-Taube Conference Center, Gunn SIEPR Building
host: King Center on Global Development and King International Development Association (KIDA)
audience: Students
summary: BRAC Enterprises' Tamara Hasan Abed discussed how social enterprise can support inclusive development.
description: Tamara Hasan Abed, Managing Director of BRAC Enterprises, discussed the role of mission-driven businesses in inclusive development. Drawing on BRAC's work in retail, dairy, agriculture, and other sectors, she explored how commercial activity can create opportunities and support social programs.

In conversation with Stanford Professor Charles Eesley, Abed considered the links between education, innovation, entrepreneurship, and equitable growth. The student-focused event was sponsored by the King Center on Global Development and KIDA.

title: Reimagining AI to Accelerate Sustainable Futures
location: See the organizer’s event page
host: Stanford Alliance on AI for the Sustainable Development Goals, King Center on Global Development, Stanford Angels & Entrepreneurs Silicon Valley, Stanford Young Alumni Bay Area, and KIDA
audience: Stanford students, alumni, and the development community
summary: A cross-sector dialogue on how AI and digital innovation can advance global development and the Sustainable Development Goals.
description: This participatory dialogue explored the contribution of AI and digital innovation to sustainable development. The invitation brought together perspectives from Stanford and development institutions working across philanthropy, policy, and implementation.

KIDA was named as a co-convenor alongside the Stanford Alliance on AI for the Sustainable Development Goals, the King Center on Global Development, Stanford Angels & Entrepreneurs Silicon Valley, and Stanford Young Alumni Bay Area. The original invitation scheduled the conversation for December 3, 2025, from 11:45 a.m. to 1 p.m. Pacific time.
series: AI for the Sustainable Development Goals

title: Research Roadmap: Doing More with Less
location: Doll 320, third floor, Gunn SIEPR Building
host: King Center on Global Development
audience: Graduate students interested in global development
summary: A faculty panel explored rigorous, cost-effective approaches to global development research when resources are limited.
description: Graduate students received practical guidance on advancing development research with limited resources and uncertain funding. Stanford faculty and researchers shared examples of designs that preserve rigor while reducing cost.

Marshall Burke discussed combining satellite imagery with existing survey data, Arun Chandrasekhar discussed efficient fieldwork design, and Duncan Lawrence introduced a WhatsApp survey tool developed by the Immigration Policy Lab. The event was part of the King Center's Research Roadmap series.

title: Global Development Graduate Student Mixer
location: Lucas Lounge, second floor, Gunn SIEPR Building
host: King Center on Global Development
audience: Graduate students from all Stanford schools
summary: Graduate students across Stanford met peers working on global development over light refreshments.
description: The King Center invited graduate students from every Stanford school to connect with one another and discuss their global development research. The mixer offered an informal opportunity to meet peers across disciplines.
The gathering took place in Lucas Lounge in the Gunn SIEPR Building, with light refreshments served.

title: Bridging Gaps, Building Futures: A Dialogue on Gender, Education, and Work
location: Koret-Taube Conference Center, Gunn SIEPR Building
host: King Center on Global Development, Pratham USA, and Center for South Asia
audience: Students, faculty, staff, and the general public
summary: Evidence from India informed a discussion of what helps women enter, remain in, and advance through paid work.
description: This panel examined why skills training alone may not enable women, particularly mothers, to remain in paid work. Drawing on evidence from India and Pratham's Second Chance program, the discussion considered continued education, childcare, household support, and spousal engagement.

Pratham's Rukmini Banerji and Stanford economist Alessandra Voena joined moderator Suhani Jalota to connect research with practical interventions that support women's employment and agency. The King Center, Pratham USA, and Center for South Asia sponsored the event.

title: Research Roadmap: Strategic Research Design
location: Koret-Taube Conference Center, Gunn SIEPR Building
host: King Center on Global Development and Stanford Impact Labs
audience: Graduate students interested in global development
summary: An interactive workshop helped students design research around partner constraints and pathways to real-world impact.
description: Stanford Impact Labs' Sarah Hopwood and Alex Carr led an interactive workshop on designing research for impact when resources are constrained. Participants brought societal problems to discuss and worked through practical frameworks for understanding partner needs and identifying opportunities.

The session connected research design decisions with a pathway from evidence to real-world change. It was jointly sponsored by Stanford Impact Labs and the King Center as part of the graduate-student Research Roadmap series.

title: 2026 Global Development Research Symposium
location: Koret-Taube Conference Center, Gunn SIEPR Building
host: King Center on Global Development, with support from the Vice Provost for Undergraduate Education and Vice Provost for Graduate Education
audience: Students, alumni, faculty, staff, and the general public
summary: Student and fellow poster presentations showcased global development research across Stanford disciplines, with a keynote by Nava Ashraf.
description: The annual symposium showcased global development research by Stanford undergraduates, predoctoral fellows, graduate students, and postdoctoral researchers, including recipients of King Center funding. Posters spanned subjects such as migration, health, food security, gender, and climate adaptation.

Nava Ashraf, Professor of Economics at the London School of Economics, delivered the lunchtime keynote. The program scheduled the keynote from noon to 12:45 p.m., followed by poster presentations from 1 to 2 p.m.

title: 2026 International Engagement Fair
location: Courtyard, Gunn SIEPR Building, 366 Galvez Street
host: King Center on Global Development, Bing Overseas Studies Program, Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies, Global Engineering Programs, and Stanford Global Studies
audience: Stanford students
summary: Meet KIDA and campus organizations offering international research, learning, and professional experiences.
description: The International Engagement Fair invites Stanford students to explore student groups and campus programs offering experiences abroad, international academic activities, and opportunities for exchange. Organizations cover fields including global health, engineering, public service, international policy, and development.

KIDA is listed among the tabling organizations. The fair is co-hosted by the King Center, Bing Overseas Studies, FSI, Global Engineering Programs, and Stanford Global Studies in the Gunn SIEPR courtyard.

title: Research Roadmap: AI and Development
location: Doll 320, third floor, Gunn SIEPR Building
host: King Center on Global Development
audience: Graduate students interested in global development
summary: Daniel Björkegren discusses AI and development, and how junior researchers can adapt their research topics and methods.
description: Daniel Björkegren, Associate Professor of International and Public Affairs at Columbia University, will discuss the intersection of AI and development. The conversation will consider how junior researchers should choose research topics and methods as the field changes.

This student event is part of the King Center's Research Roadmap series, which offers research and career advice for graduate students interested in global development. Lunch will be served; registration is available through the official event page.

title: Doing Development Differently: Lessons from BRAC on Local Leadership and Global Scale
location: Koret-Taube Conference Center, Gunn SIEPR Building
host: King Center on Global Development and BRAC
audience: Students, alumni, faculty, staff, and the general public
summary: BRAC Executive Director Asif Saleh explores local leadership, stronger systems, and development amid a changing aid landscape.
description: Asif Saleh, Executive Director of BRAC, will discuss how global development is changing as foreign aid declines and global crises overlap. Drawing on BRAC's experience, the conversation will examine locally led solutions, durable capacity, and approaches grounded in communities' priorities.

The event will consider how development organizations can rethink funding, delivery, and collaboration while sustaining impact. Sponsored by the King Center and BRAC as part of Food for Thought, the event includes dinner and registration through the official listing.

title: Overcoming Barriers to Women’s Political Participation: Evidence from Nigeria
location: Online; Stanford ID and room access required for in-person attendance in Encina Hall, Philippines Conference Room
host: Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL)
audience: Public online; Stanford affiliates with room access in person
summary: Claire Adida discussed experimental evidence on collective agency and women’s participation in local governance.
description: Claire Adida presented a randomized evaluation involving women’s action committees in 300 communities in southwest Nigeria. The research compared basic civic education with additional training intended to strengthen women’s collective efficacy.

The seminar examined changes in women’s participation, their perceptions of local leaders’ responsiveness, and the role of individual and collective agency. Hesham Sallam moderated. Online participation was public; in-person attendance required an active Stanford ID and access to the conference room.

title: Foreign Aid and the Performance of Bureaucrats
location: Online; Stanford ID and room access required for Encina Hall, E-008
host: Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL)
audience: Public online; Stanford affiliates with room access in person
summary: Maria Nagawa examined how donor-funded projects reshape bureaucrats’ incentives and state capacity.
description: Drawing on interviews, surveys, and survey experiments with more than 600 Ugandan bureaucrats, Maria Nagawa examined how project-based foreign aid changes working conditions and staff incentives.

The talk explored a tension between improved performance on donor projects and the diversion of effort from ordinary government duties, alongside effects on equity and teamwork. Hesham Sallam moderated. Virtual attendance was public; in-person access was limited to Stanford ID holders able to enter the room.

title: Seeing Green: The Effects of Financial Exposures on Support for Climate Action
location: Online; Stanford ID and room access required for William J. Perry Conference Room, Encina Hall
host: Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL)
audience: Public online; Stanford affiliates with room access in person
summary: Saumitra Jha presented an experiment on financial-market exposure and support for climate policy.
description: Saumitra Jha examined whether opportunities to trade green and brown energy stocks can encourage learning about climate change and alter support for mitigation policies.

The randomized study connected financial exposure with changes in climate beliefs, donations, and personal decisions. The seminar offered an example of using experimental research to study the political economy of the green transition. Hesham Sallam moderated; the online session was open to the public.

title: Let Them Be Warned Not to Play With Fire: Understanding Electoral Repression in Zimbabwe
location: Online; Stanford ID and room access required for Encina Hall, E-008
host: Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL)
audience: Public online; Stanford affiliates with room access in person
summary: Lauren Young investigated when rulers use electoral violence and the constraints on that strategy.
description: Using evidence from 25 years of elections in Zimbabwe, Lauren Young examined why autocrats may avoid electoral violence and turn to it as a last resort.

The seminar considered unpredictable citizen responses, the organization of coercion, and the difficulty of scaling violence back once security forces become involved. These questions bear on accountable institutions and the protection of political participation. Hesham Sallam moderated; public participation was available online.

title: Global Debt and its Discontents
location: Online
host: Stanford Global Studies Division
audience: Everyone; free online registration
summary: An interdisciplinary dialogue examined debt relief, financial power, and responsibilities toward poorer countries.
description: Hannah Appel, Jayati Ghosh, and Fabio Vighi joined moderator Jisha Menon to examine global indebtedness and the political, ethical, and economic questions surrounding debt forgiveness.

The conversation connected sovereign debt to inequality, colonial histories, health disparities, climate pressures, and the authority to decide whose obligations can be forgiven. The event was sponsored by Stanford Global Studies and cross-listed by International Relations. The central Stanford calendar identifies the virtual event as free and open to everyone.

title: Unfinished Business: Marcel Fafchamps’ Livestreamed Keynote
location: Online via Zoom; the full in-person symposium was invitation only
host: Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL) and King Center on Global Development
audience: Public virtual keynote; in-person symposium by invitation only
summary: A livestreamed keynote celebrated Marcel Fafchamps’ contributions to development economics.
description: The public-facing portion of this symposium featured Marcel Fafchamps’ keynote, “Behavioral Markets,” followed by an opportunity for virtual attendees to share remarks. The event recognized his work on institutions, social networks, and market failures in lower-income countries.

The broader symposium included research on management, employment, mutual aid, and socioeconomic status. Its in-person sessions were invitation only. This listing is specifically for the livestreamed keynote, beginning at 9:00 a.m. Pacific, rather than an invitation to the full in-person program.

title: Innovating GRIPP for Governance, Human Security, and Sustainable Development
location: Online; Stanford ID and room access required for Encina Hall, Philippines Conference Room
host: Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL)
audience: Public online; Stanford affiliates with room access in person
summary: Sanjeev Khagram introduced a prototype AI platform for analyzing resilience and development risks.
description: Sanjeev Khagram introduced the Global Resilience Intelligence Platform and Partnership, a prototype intended to support decisions about governance, human security, and sustainable development.

The seminar described country-level forecasting, scenario analysis, hotspot detection, and AI-assisted explanations, with an initial focus on political resilience, fragility, conflict, and violence. Kathryn Stoner moderated. The session was open to the public virtually; in-person attendance required an active Stanford ID and access to the conference room.

title: Why Women Leave: Gendered Pathways of Global Talent
location: Encina Hall, Philippines Conference Room (C330), 3rd floor
host: Walter H. Shorenstein Asia-Pacific Research Center (APARC) · Korea Program and Stanford Next Asia Policy Lab
audience: General public
summary: Minyoung An examined how gender inequality shapes skilled migration and return pathways.
description: This seminar explored the interaction between structural gender inequality and individual aspirations in international talent migration. Using South Korea as a case, Minyoung An examined differences in the educational selectivity of women and men moving to the United States.

The talk also introduced comparative work on Korea and Taiwan concerning return migration among U.S.-trained PhDs. It connected talent circulation to gendered opportunities and constraints. The Stanford calendar identifies the event as free and open to the general public.

title: Islamic Environmental Ethics and Multispecies Responsibility in Southeast Asia
location: Encina Hall, Philippines Conference Room, 3rd floor
host: Walter H. Shorenstein Asia-Pacific Research Center (APARC) and Sohaib and Sara Abbasi Program in Islamic Studies
audience: Students and general public; registration available
summary: Teren Sevea explored local environmental knowledge and ethical responses to ecological change in Southeast Asia.
description: Teren Sevea examined how everyday Islamic practices and local understandings in Southeast Asia respond to ecological crisis, extraction, and rapid developmental change.

The discussion considered relationships between communities, environments, and other species, including both care and exploitation. It asked what environmental responsibility can learn from situated ethical traditions and local knowledge. The Stanford calendar explicitly included undergraduate and graduate students and the general public among eligible audiences.

title: Foreign Aid and the Performance of Bureaucrats
location: Encina Commons, Room 123, 615 Crothers Way, Stanford
host: Center for African Studies and Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL)
audience: Everyone
summary: Maria Nagawa discussed the institutional consequences of project-based aid, drawing on research in Uganda.
description: This April presentation examined how foreign aid affects the bureaucracies responsible for sustained public-service delivery. Maria Nagawa drew on interviews, surveys, and survey experiments with Ugandan bureaucrats to explain how donor projects can redirect effort and reshape workplace relationships.

The session considered why incentives that improve donor-funded work may weaken routine state functions and organizational cohesion. It was hosted by the Center for African Studies with CDDRL. The central Stanford calendar lists the audience as everyone; this was a separate presentation from the October 2025 CDDRL seminar.

title: The Drivers and Consequences of the International Mobility of Healthcare Professionals from the Philippines
location: Encina Hall, Philippines Conference Room (C330), 3rd floor
host: Walter H. Shorenstein Asia-Pacific Research Center (APARC) · Asia Health Policy Program
audience: Stanford undergraduate and graduate students, postdocs, faculty, staff, affiliates, and alumni
summary: Marjorie Pajaron examined healthcare-worker migration, climate risks, and the balance between brain drain and human-capital gains.
description: This research seminar considered the drivers and effects of Filipino healthcare professionals’ international mobility, including climate-related pressures and the consequences for the domestic health workforce.

Marjorie Pajaron examined possible shortages and uneven distribution of skilled workers alongside gains from remittances, training incentives, and return migration. Karen Eggleston moderated. The central Stanford calendar explicitly included undergraduate and graduate students; the event was free with registration.

title: El Salvador: A Carceral State of Terror — Screening and Discussion
location: William J. Perry Conference Room, Encina Hall, 2nd floor; public livestream via Zoom
host: Democracy Action Lab and Poverty, Violence, and Governance Lab, Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL)
audience: Stanford affiliates in person; public online
summary: A research-based screening explored the social and institutional consequences of El Salvador’s state of exception.
description: A short film grounded in Beatriz Magaloni’s field research opened a discussion of mass detention, civil liberties, and democratic institutions in El Salvador. Speakers included Noah Bullock, Beatriz Magaloni, and Manuel Ortiz, with Alberto Díaz-Cayeros moderating.

The event examined how security policy affects low-income families, due process, and political accountability, combining qualitative research with practitioner perspectives. In-person attendance was for Stanford affiliates; the host also offered a public Zoom livestream.
series: Democracy Action Lab · Poverty, Violence, and Governance Lab

title: Climate Shocks, Household Food Security, and Welfare in Afghanistan
location: Online
host: Abbasi Program in Islamic Studies, Center for South Asia, and Center on Food Security and the Environment
audience: Everyone; free online registration
summary: Hayatullah Ahmadzai examined how climate shocks affect agricultural households’ welfare and food security.
description: This talk used two household surveys to study the effects of climate shocks, particularly flooding, on agricultural households in Afghanistan, while accounting for conflict and price shocks.

Hayatullah Ahmadzai discussed implications for disaster-risk reduction and planning to help vulnerable households respond to and recover from environmental shocks. The event was cross-listed by International Relations and sponsored by the Abbasi Program, Center for South Asia, and Center on Food Security and the Environment. The Stanford calendar identifies it as free and open to everyone online.

title: Long-Term Care Insurance Policy Changes and Healthcare Utilization in South Korea
location: Encina Hall, Philippines Conference Room (C330)
host: Walter H. Shorenstein Asia-Pacific Research Center (APARC) · Asia Health Policy Program
audience: Stanford undergraduate and graduate students, postdocs, faculty, staff, affiliates, and alumni
summary: Eunkyeong Lee examined how expanded long-term-care coverage changed healthcare use and spending.
description: The seminar assessed long-term-care insurance expansions in South Korea using nationwide claims from 2006–2019. It considered whether greater access to long-term care substitutes for hospital services or complements outpatient care.

Eunkyeong Lee discussed reduced hospital use alongside increased dementia-related outpatient visits, and the implications for health-system efficiency and an aging population. The official Stanford calendar explicitly included undergraduate and graduate students among eligible attendees.

title: Building Dictatorships: Legitimacy and Large-Scale Infrastructure
location: Online; Stanford ID and room access required for Encina Hall, East, E-008
host: Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL)
audience: Public online; Stanford affiliates with room access in person
summary: Chris Dann examines how infrastructure delivery affects perceptions of government performance under autocracy.
description: Chris Dann studies how large construction projects can create reputations for economic delivery and strengthen political legitimacy without democratic reform.

The presentation draws on geolocated infrastructure projects and harmonized survey data to examine how effective delivery changes perceptions of government performance. It connects public investment to the social contract and the institutional conditions of development. Hesham Sallam moderates. Virtual attendance is public; in-person participation requires an active Stanford ID and room access.

title: Directional AI Advice: Experimental Evidence from Healthcare
location: Online via Zoom
host: Walter H. Shorenstein Asia-Pacific Research Center (APARC) · Asia Health Policy Program
audience: Stanford undergraduate and graduate students, postdocs, faculty, staff, affiliates, and alumni; free registration
summary: Lingsheng Meng presents experimental evidence on how AI advice changes patient–physician interactions and healthcare use.
description: This seminar examines a preregistered field experiment at a Chinese hospital in which patients received access to an AI chatbot before outpatient appointments.

The study explores how directional advice can affect prescribing, diagnostic tests, patient compliance, and satisfaction, and how those effects interact with physicians’ practices. Lingsheng Meng presents the research. The session is online, free, and explicitly open to undergraduate and graduate students according to the Stanford calendar.

title: Authoritarian Aid and Democratic Attitudes: Backlash, Not Diffusion
location: Online; Stanford ID and room access required for Encina Hall, East, E-008
host: Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL)
audience: Public online; Stanford affiliates with room access in person
summary: Marcela Ibáñez examines how exposure to Chinese development finance shapes democratic attitudes in Latin America.
description: Marcela Ibáñez presents research on whether an authoritarian donor’s local development projects change citizens’ commitment to democracy. The study uses geocoded evidence from Chinese development finance in Latin America.

The paper challenges a simple diffusion account, instead examining when visible projects may heighten accountability demands on recipient-country leaders. The seminar connects development finance, political institutions, and causal research. Hesham Sallam moderates; public attendance is available virtually, while in-person access requires a Stanford ID and room access.

title: Cross-National Comparison of Long-Term Care Fraud Oversight and Investigation Practices
location: Encina Hall, Philippines Conference Room (C330), 3rd floor
host: Walter H. Shorenstein Asia-Pacific Research Center (APARC) · Asia Health Policy Program
audience: Stanford undergraduate and graduate students, postdocs, faculty, staff, affiliates, and alumni; free registration
summary: Hyunkyung “Yulia” Yun compares safeguards against misuse of long-term-care resources in the United States, Japan, and South Korea.
description: The seminar compares how long-term-care systems identify suspicious billing, investigate potential fraud, recover improper payments, and coordinate enforcement.

Hyunkyung “Yulia” Yun considers transferable lessons from the United States, Japan, and South Korea, emphasizing protection of public resources and continuity of care for residents. The discussion connects health-system governance with sustainable social protection. The Stanford calendar explicitly includes undergraduate and graduate students and provides free registration.

title: Delivering Humanitarian Aid in a Contested World
location: Bechtel Conference Center, Encina Hall; reception in Coit D. Blacker Lobby
host: Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL) with IsraAID and partners
audience: Active Stanford students, faculty, researchers, and staff; registration required
summary: Two panels explore the practical challenges of delivering humanitarian relief and regional cooperation.
description: This event brings IsraAID and partners together to discuss humanitarian assistance where access, neutrality, and safety are uncertain. The first panel examines global operational challenges; the second considers Arab-Israeli cooperation in aid delivery across the Middle East.

The program includes practitioners from humanitarian and medical-relief organizations, with discussions moderated by Stanford faculty. Attendance requires registration and is limited to active Stanford students, faculty, researchers, and staff. The host plans to publish a recording of the introduction and first panel afterward.

title: Stanford Conference on Environmental Entrepreneurship
location: Stanford campus
host: Stanford Graduate School of Business
audience: Students, faculty, staff, Stanford community, alumni, and public; event registration or application requirements apply.
summary: Research and practice on building a sustainable economy through social and commercial entrepreneurship.
description: Researchers and practitioners came together to examine how entrepreneurship can contribute to a sustainable world economy. The conference treated entrepreneurship broadly, including social ventures and commercial enterprises.

The call welcomed contributions from the public sector, NGOs, nonprofit organizations, and startups across the world. The event was part of Stanford GSB’s Sustainability Research Conference Series; the original page includes the agenda and a discussion of the conference takeaways.

title: Indigenous Stewardship for Sustainability
location: Stanford Graduate School of Business
host: Stanford Graduate School of Business
audience: Students, faculty, staff, Stanford community, alumni, and public; event registration or application requirements apply.
summary: Scholars and practitioners examined Indigenous land stewardship, land return, and their wider benefits.
description: The conference explored the impacts, challenges, and opportunities of returning land to local Indigenous communities and revitalizing stewardship led by tribes.

Organized by Tadashi Fukami and Raven Longwolf Alcott, it brought together academic researchers, Indigenous leaders, cultural practitioners, and land stewardship organizations. The official page explicitly welcomed all interested participants and provides an agenda and post-conference discussion.

title: Sustainable and Responsible Operations in the Age of AI
location: Stanford campus
host: Stanford Graduate School of Business
audience: Students, faculty, staff, and Stanford community. Historical event; registration is closed.
summary: A one-day conference on AI, environmental stewardship, sustainable supply chains, and socially responsible public systems.
description: Academics and practitioners examined how data and AI can support sustainability, resilience, and social responsibility. Sessions considered satellite monitoring of forests, carbon and land-use accounting, sustainable value chains, and the energy demands of AI.

The agenda also addressed education policy, fairness in homeless services, agriculture, and governance. Organized by Dan A. Iancu as part of the GSB sustainability conference series, the event ran from 8:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m.; the official page now marks registration as closed.

title: Civil Society and Sustainability Conference
location: Stanford campus
host: Stanford Graduate School of Business · Center on Philanthropy and Civil Society
audience: Students, faculty, staff, Stanford community, alumni, and public. Historical event; applications are closed.
summary: A conference on how nonprofits, community organizations, activists, and philanthropists advance sustainability.
description: This conference brought researchers and practitioners together to study the contributions of civil society to sustainability. Its focus included nonprofits, activists, community organizations, and philanthropy.

Stanford GSB partnered with the Center on Philanthropy and Civil Society, with the King Center on Global Development listed as a co-sponsor. Patricia Bromley organized the conference. The original page provides the agenda and speaker biographies and indicates that applications for the 2026 event are closed.

title: Using AI in Law and Policy Research
location: Online
host: Stanford Law School · Law and Policy Lab
audience: Open to the Stanford community, including non-law students; RSVP through the official page.
summary: Build a practical methodology for using AI in law and policy research.
description: The Robert Crown Law Library reference team will introduce approaches to using AI tools effectively in policy and legal research. The session highlights the Stanford Law AI Initiative website, library resources, and available training.

The workshop is open to the Stanford community. The event page asks participants to obtain approval from their faculty and policy clients before incorporating AI into research. RSVP through the original page.
series: Law and Policy Lab Skills Workshops

title: Introduction to Systems Thinking
location: Stanford Law School, Room 14
host: Stanford Law School · Law and Policy Lab
audience: Open to the Stanford community, including non-law students; RSVP through the official page.
summary: Learn to identify interconnected causes, policy effects, and unintended consequences through systems thinking.
description: Professor Paul Brest will introduce systems thinking as an approach to understanding complex public problems and designing policy for durable improvement. The discussion considers links among multiple causes, institutions, and downstream effects.

Examples in the event description include environmental regulation, homelessness, racism, vaccine distribution, and criminal justice. The workshop is open to the Stanford community, and participants are expected to complete approximately one hour of preparation. RSVP and preparation details are available through the original event page.
series: Law and Policy Lab Skills Workshops

title: Writing Policy Reports and Using AI for Drafting
location: Stanford Law School, Room 14
host: Stanford Law School · Law and Policy Lab
audience: Open to the Stanford community, including non-law students; RSVP through the official page.
summary: Practice turning research and data into clear policy reports, memos, and briefing papers.
description: Policy Lab Program Director Luciana Herman and Crown Library Associate Director Taryn Marks will teach approaches to organizing evidence into effective policy reports and briefing papers, including the use of AI in drafting.

Using past Policy Lab projects and case-study principles associated with Robert K. Yin, the session considers context, process, and the distinction between empirical policy analysis and legal advocacy. It forms part of Elements of Policy Analysis and is open to everyone in the Stanford community.
series: Law and Policy Lab Skills Workshops

title: Oral Briefings for Public Policy
location: Stanford Law School, Room 21
host: Stanford Law School · Law and Policy Lab
audience: Open to the Stanford community, including non-law students; RSVP through the official page.
summary: Practice the structure and delivery of an effective briefing for a policy client.
description: This participatory workshop offers a setting to rehearse public speaking before presenting to a policy client. Attendees may bring a policy topic of their own or use a mock topic.

The session focuses on the style and structure of an effective policy briefing. It is offered by the Stanford Law and Policy Lab and is open to the Stanford community. Registration information is linked from the original event page.
series: Law and Policy Lab Skills Workshops

title: Writing Op-Eds, Blogs & Opinion Pieces
location: Stanford Law School, Room 21
host: Stanford Law School · Law and Policy Lab
audience: Open to the Stanford community, including non-law students; RSVP through the official page.
summary: Explore how to communicate research through op-eds, blogs, and opinion writing.
description: The Law and Policy Lab will host a discussion about translating research into public-facing advocacy. Participants are encouraged to bring ideas for opinion writing.

The workshop considers the structure and style of effective advocacy using op-eds and Substack posts by Stanford professors and colleagues. The event is open to the Stanford community and provides an RSVP link on its original page.
series: Law and Policy Lab Skills Workshops

title: The Political Economics of Sustainability
location: Stanford Graduate School of Business, Stanford, CA
host: Stanford Graduate School of Business
audience: Faculty and students; apply to attend through the official event page.
summary: A research conference on political constraints and economic policy design for the green transition.
description: The conference examines how political forces shape environmental policy, regulation, and the prospects for a sustainable transition. Its premise is that policies must remain politically viable both when introduced and over time.

Leading scholars will discuss theoretical and empirical approaches to designing sustainable policies. Bård Harstad and Allan Hsiao organize the event within Stanford GSB’s Sustainability Research Conference Series. Students are included in the stated audience; an application to attend is linked from the original page.

title: Marketing for Sustainability
location: Stanford, CA
host: Stanford Graduate School of Business
audience: Faculty and students; apply to attend. Presenter submissions are due October 30, 2026.
summary: Research on how consumers, firms, markets, and public policy can advance environmental, social, and economic sustainability.
description: The third Marketing for Sustainability Conference explores how marketing and related research can support environmental protection and social and economic wellbeing. Topics include sustainable products, consumer decisions, market barriers, and the design of public policy.

The conference welcomes empirical and theoretical work in marketing, economics, and related fields, with discussion following each presentation. Faculty and students are listed as eligible audiences. The official page links an attendance application and asks prospective presenters to submit an extended abstract or paper by October 30, 2026.

title: Technology, Forced Labor, and the Uyghur Genocide
location: Encina Commons 123, 615 Crothers Way
host: Abbasi Program in Islamic Studies, Center for Human Rights and International Justice, Center for East Asian Studies, and Hoover Institution
audience: Everyone; free event
summary: Rushan Abbas and Glenn Tiffert examined surveillance, forced labor, and human rights in global supply chains.
description: The program examined connections between surveillance technologies, AI-enabled policing, forced labor, and repression of Uyghur communities. Opening remarks by Glenn Tiffert considered research systems and the international spread of repressive technologies.

Rushan Abbas connected these systems to Uyghur families' experiences and global supply chains. A joint question-and-answer discussion addressed technology, governance, and accountability. The Stanford calendar listed this free event as open to everyone.

title: Careers in International Law and Policy
location: Encina Hall, Suite 030, 616 Jane Stanford Way
host: Center for Human Rights and International Justice
audience: Stanford students; RSVP required
summary: Stanford scholars discussed routes into careers in international law, human rights, and public policy.
description: This student career workshop brought together Beth Van Schaack, Julia Spiegel, and E. Tendayi Achiume, with Penelope Van Tuyl moderating. The panel offered guidance on pursuing careers in international law and policy.

Their work spans human rights, migration, accountability, and public service. Attendance was limited to Stanford students, with an RSVP required and lunch provided. The listing gives a start time but does not specify an end time.

title: Unearthed: Social and Environmental Costs of Mining for Battery Minerals
location: Mitchell Earth Sciences, Hartley Conference Room, 397 Panama Mall
host: Center for Human Rights and International Justice and Precourt Institute for Energy
audience: Free campus event; RSVP for lunch
summary: Brad Adams discussed community-centered investigations of the human rights costs of battery mineral supply chains.
description: Climate Rights International's Brad Adams discussed the social and environmental costs of mining minerals used in electric vehicles and electricity grids. Community-centered investigations provided a starting point for examining human rights risks in the energy transition.

The lunchtime discussion considered implications and possible responses. Precourt Institute for Energy and the Center for Human Rights and International Justice co-hosted the event; the Stanford calendar listed it as free, with registration and lunch upon RSVP.

title: Building a New Data Infrastructure for the 21st Century
location: CoDa W101
host: Stanford Program in Data Science
audience: Students and the Data Science community; RSVP requested
summary: David Grusky considered how to improve the social survey and build tools for monitoring social conditions.
description: The Program in Data Science invited Professor David Grusky to discuss the limitations facing the century-old social survey and possibilities for a better monitoring tool. The talk formed part of the Listen. Engage. Connect. series.

Grusky directs Stanford's Center on Poverty and Inequality and studies the measurement of poverty, inequality, and mobility. This methods-focused conversation is relevant to students interested in how evidence informs social policy. Lunch was provided and an RSVP was requested.

title: Data Science Faculty Lunch: David Lobell
location: Stanford Faculty Club, 439 Lagunita Drive
host: Stanford Program in Data Science, supported by VPUE's Academic-Residential Co-Curriculum program
audience: Stanford undergraduate students; limited sign-up, one faculty lunch per student
summary: An undergraduate faculty lunch with David Lobell, whose research connects food security, agriculture, and climate.
description: Students joined Earth System Science Professor David Lobell for an informal lunch at the Stanford Faculty Club. The program offered a chance to learn about his research, discuss students' interests, and build a faculty connection outside class.

Lobell's official research profile focuses on food security, agricultural adaptation to climate change, and the use of large datasets. The lunch belonged to an undergraduate mentoring initiative supported by VPUE. Students were asked to sign up for only one faculty lunch.

title: Data Science Faculty Lunch: sean reardon
location: Stanford Faculty Club, 439 Lagunita Drive
host: Stanford Program in Data Science, supported by VPUE's Academic-Residential Co-Curriculum program
audience: Stanford undergraduate students; five student places, sign-up required
summary: Five students joined education researcher sean reardon for a small faculty lunch and mentoring conversation.
description: The Program in Data Science offered five students an informal lunch with Professor sean reardon at the Stanford Faculty Club. Students could learn about his work, share their interests, and make a connection outside the classroom.

Reardon's research examines social and educational inequality, segregation, achievement gaps, and methods for measuring unequal opportunity. The event was part of a VPUE-supported initiative designed to strengthen undergraduates' professional relationships and mentorship with Stanford faculty.

title: The Highest Exam: How the Gaokao Shapes China
location: Bechtel Conference Center, Encina Hall, 616 Jane Stanford Way; livestream also available
host: Stanford Center on China's Economy and Institutions
audience: Stanford community and public audiences; in-person registration or livestream
summary: Ruixue Jia and Hongbin Li discussed how China's entrance exam shapes education, mobility, and society.
description: Authors Ruixue Jia and Hongbin Li discussed their book The Highest Exam in a fireside chat. The conversation examined the gaokao as an institution shaping family decisions, education, socioeconomic opportunity, and China's wider economy.

The event combined an in-person conversation at Encina Hall with a livestream for remote audiences. In-person participants were invited to a reception and a book signing with Hongbin Li afterward. The discussion connected education policy with inequality and economic development.

title: Energy Management and Systems Change in Factories and Supply Chains in China
location: Goldman Room E409, Encina Hall, 616 Jane Stanford Way
host: Stanford Center on China's Economy and Institutions
audience: Registered attendees interested in China's economy and sustainability; no degree restriction stated
summary: Valerie Karplus examined industrial energy use, management decisions, and sustainability incentives across Chinese supply chains.
description: Valerie Karplus presented a framework for evaluating the economic and environmental effects of industrial production systems. The research considered interventions in iron and steel production, metal components manufacturing, and automotive assembly.

The seminar connected observations of factory decisions with the incentives shaping sustainability progress across supply chains. SCCEI publicly offered registration to attend and described lunch and calendar reminders. Its listing states no degree or department requirement for attendees.

title: Young Children at Risk of Poor Development in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
location: Goldman Room E409, Encina Hall, 616 Jane Stanford Way
host: Stanford Center on Early Childhood and Rural Education Action Program, listed by the Stanford Center on China's Economy and Institutions
audience: Registered attendees interested in early childhood development; no degree restriction stated
summary: Chunling Lu presented updated measures of childhood exposure to poverty, stunting, and related developmental risks.
description: Harvard global health researcher Chunling Lu discussed updated global, regional, and country estimates of young children's exposure to developmental risks. The research revisited earlier estimates using newer data and poverty definitions.

The seminar considered trends since 2000 and disparities in risk exposure, with implications for evidence-based early childhood policy. Stanford's Center on Early Childhood and Rural Education Action Program hosted the conversation. Registration was offered publicly and lunch was provided.

title: The Risks of Taiwan's Economic Boom
location: Bender Room, Green Library, Bing Wing, fifth floor, 459 Lasuen Mall; online attendance available
host: Stanford University Libraries and Stanford Center on China's Economy and Institutions
audience: In-person or online registrants; no degree restriction stated
summary: Chang-Tai Hsieh examined export-led growth, exchange-rate policy, and financial risks in Taiwan's economy.
description: The 2026 Dr. Sam-Chung Hsieh Memorial Lecture featured economist Chang-Tai Hsieh. He examined how Taiwan's exchange-rate policy interacted with export growth and its central position in semiconductor and AI hardware production.

The lecture considered the financial vulnerabilities accompanying large trade surpluses and foreign asset holdings. Stanford Libraries and SCCEI offered both in-person and online registration. The event provides a comparative perspective on the institutions and tradeoffs involved in economic growth.

title: Corporate ESG Actions: Evidence from a Nationwide Experiment in China
location: Goldman Room E409, Encina Hall, 616 Jane Stanford Way
host: Stanford Center on China's Economy and Institutions
audience: Registration required; no attendee degree restriction stated
summary: Guojun He presents experimental evidence on investor demand, corporate ESG reporting, and environmental performance in China.
description: Guojun He will discuss a nationwide field experiment involving more than 4,800 listed firms in China. The study uses public investor questions to examine how environmental, social, and governance concerns change corporate responses and behavior.

The research connects investor demand with disclosure, environmental performance, and firm valuations. SCCEI lists the talk in its fall seminar series and provides a public Register to Attend link. Students interested in environmental governance and empirical development research can consult the host's registration page.

title: From Free Rider to Innovator: The Rise of China's Drug Development
location: Goldman Room E409, Encina Hall, 616 Jane Stanford Way
host: Stanford Center on China's Economy and Institutions
audience: Registration required; no attendee degree restriction stated
summary: Panle Jia Barwick examines how Chinese reimbursement reform shaped pharmaceutical innovation and access to medicines.
description: Panle Jia Barwick will present research on China's expanding role in drug development and clinical trials. The study combines information across the pharmaceutical supply chain to investigate the policy changes behind that transformation.

The seminar focuses on the National Reimbursement Drug List reform and the relationship between drug affordability, market size, and incentives for innovation. SCCEI publicly offers registration to attend; the event listing does not impose a degree or departmental restriction.

title: Decoding China's Industrial Policies
location: Goldman Room E409, Encina Hall, 616 Jane Stanford Way
host: Stanford Center on China's Economy and Institutions
audience: Registered seminar attendees; historical registration closed at capacity
summary: Hanming Fang examined China's industrial policy using a large database of government documents and firm data.
description: Hanming Fang presented research using language models to analyze industrial-policy documents issued by central, provincial, and municipal governments in China. The project linked policy objectives, instruments, and implementation patterns to firm behavior.

The seminar considered productivity, political economy, and potential costs such as overcapacity and spatial inefficiency. SCCEI's archive notes that high interest exhausted room capacity and registration closed. It belongs to the fall 2025 seminar archive, rather than an event currently accepting registrations.

title: Hamilton's Nightmare: Financial Repression, Political Control, and Local Debt in China
location: Goldman Room E409, Encina Hall, 616 Jane Stanford Way
host: Stanford Center on China's Economy and Institutions
audience: Registered seminar attendees; historical registration closed at capacity
summary: Victor Shih examined how financial repression and central-local political relations shape China's local-government debt.
description: Victor Shih discussed the incentives behind local-government borrowing in China. The research connected expectations of central bailouts and financial repression with the way local authorities respond to fiscal pressure.

The analysis considered debt refinancing and additional borrowing after floods and other stresses. The seminar offered a perspective on public finance and institutions that influence development and disaster recovery. SCCEI's archive notes registration closed because of capacity; it is presented here as a past event.
